extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of differential equations / dynamical systems (upper-undergraduate or beginning graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and criteria for analyzing limit sets, closed orbits, local flow structure, and stability in planar autonomous systems (definitions, propositions, Poincaré map, and the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem). Also elementary applications (e.g., SIR models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic solution (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonequilibrium point X is a periodic solution if there exists τ > 0 with φ_τ(X) = X; the least such τ > 0 is the period. Then φ_{t+τ}(X)=φ_t(X) for all t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: all nonzero solutions of the undamped harmonic oscillator are periodic. Periodic solutions may attract other solutions (limit cycles).

rubrics_metrics.name: ω-limit and α-limit sets (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Y is an ω-limit point of the solution through X if there exists a sequence t_n → ∞ with φ_{t_n}(X) → Y. The ω-limit set ω(X) is the set of all such points. α-limits defined similarly using t_n → −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an asymptotically stable equilibrium is the ω-limit set of points in its basin; any equilibrium is its own α- and ω-limit; a periodic solution is the α- and ω-limit of every point on it and may be the ω-limit of other points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: invariance and containment properties of limit sets
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) If X and Z lie on the same solution then ω(X)=ω(Z) and α(X)=α(Z). 2) If D is closed and positively invariant and Z ∈ D, then ω(Z) ⊂ D (and similarly for negative invariance and α-limits). 3) A closed invariant set contains the α- and ω-limit sets of every point in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are structural constraints used repeatedly (proofs by flow invariance and continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local section (transverse line) (definition & property)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a non-equilibrium point X_0, the transverse line Σ(X_0) is the straight line through X_0 perpendicular to F(X_0). A local section S is an open subinterval of this transverse line where the vector field is not tangent, so solutions cross S transversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameterized by h(u)=X_0+uV_0 with V_0 unit vector perpendicular to F(X_0). At each point of S the vector field points 'away from' S, so trajectories cut S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow box (construction & property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a local section S at X_0, define Ψ(s,u)=φ_s(h(u)) mapping a neighborhood N of the origin in R^2 to a neighborhood of X_0. For small N this Ψ is one-to-one and provides coordinates in which horizontal lines map to solution arcs and vertical lines to S; V_σ=Ψ(N) is the flow box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the flow box, solutions behave like parallel straight lines at constant speed; DΨ maps the constant vector (1,0) to F(X). Important property: if X∈V_σ then φ_t(X)∈S for a unique t∈(−σ,σ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of first arrival time to a local section
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a local section and φ_{t_0}(Z_0)=X_0∈S, then there is a neighborhood U of Z_0 and a continuous function τ:U→R with τ(Z_0)=t_0 such that φ_{τ(X)}(X) ∈ S for each X∈U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the function G(X,t)=φ_t(X)·F(X_0) and the Implicit Function Theorem because ∂G/∂t at (Z_0,t_0) equals |F(X_0)|^2 ≠ 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré map (first return map) (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed orbit γ and X_0∈γ with a local section S at X_0, the Poincaré map P takes X∈S to P(X)=φ_t(X)∈S where t>0 is the smallest positive return time (first return).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P may not be defined at all points of S (solutions might never return), but P(X_0)=X_0 and P is C^1 near X_0 by the Implicit Function Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability criterion via derivative of the Poincaré map
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a Poincaré map defined on a neighborhood of X_0 in S and |P'(X_0)| < 1, then the closed orbit γ is asymptotically stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locally P(x)=a x + higher-order terms with |a|<1, so iterates move points closer to 0 (X_0), meaning trajectories approach γ each return. Example: compute P' for r'=r(1−r), θ'=1 to show P'(1)=e^{-2π}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: monotone sequence along a solution or segment
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite/infinite sequence X_0,X_1,... on a solution is monotone along the solution if φ_{t_n}(X_0)=X_n with 0≤t_1<t_2<... . A sequence Y_n on a segment I is monotone along I if Yn is between Yn−1 and Yn+1 in the natural order on I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sequence can be monotone along a solution but not along a segment and vice versa; this cannot happen if the segment is a local section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: monotonicity along solution implies monotonicity along local section
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a local section and Y_0,Y_1,Y_2,... are distinct points in S lying on the same solution curve, then monotonicity along the solution implies monotonicity along S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the simple closed curve built from the solution arc and the segment of S and positive invariance of the exterior region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: ω-limit point crosses a local section at most once
rubrics_metrics.description: For a planar system, if Y ∈ ω(X) then the solution through Y crosses any local section at no more than one point (same for α(X)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if it crossed twice one finds disjoint flow-box intervals which the solution visits infinitely often, producing a monotone sequence that cannot be monotone along the section — contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré–Bendixson Theorem (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ω(X) is a nonempty, closed, and bounded limit set of a planar system that contains no equilibrium point, then ω(X) is a closed orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: in the plane, closed bounded limit sets are either equilibria, closed orbits, or made up of equilibria and connecting orbits (heteroclinic/homoclinic). Proof uses local sections, flow boxes, and monotone sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of limit cycles and spiraling property
rubrics_metrics.description: A limit cycle is a closed orbit γ such that γ ⊂ ω(X) or γ ⊂ α(X) for some X ∉ γ. If γ is an ω-limit cycle and γ=ω(X) with X∈γ then some solution spirals toward γ as t→∞ and there is a neighborhood of initial points whose ω-limit is γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all closed orbits are limit cycles (e.g., linear centers). The spiraling gives one-sided stability and yields an open set {Y | ω(Y)=γ} − γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: invariance implies equilibrium or limit cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is a closed, bounded set that is positively (or negatively) invariant and X∈K, then ω(X) lies in K; hence such K contains either an equilibrium point or a limit cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deduce existence of closed orbits or equilibria in invariant regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: region bounded by a closed orbit contains equilibrium or limit cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ is a closed orbit and U is the open region in the interior of γ, then U contains either an equilibrium point or a limit cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via invariance and Poincaré–Bendixson; can be sharpened to show U must contain an equilibrium (Corollary 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: boundary closed orbit implies interior equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ is a closed orbit that forms the boundary of an open set U, then U contains an equilibrium point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by considering minimal-area enclosed regions and ruling out infinitely many closed orbits via limit arguments and Corollary 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: first integral constantness forbids limit cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: If H is a first integral of a planar system and H is not constant on any open set, then there are no limit cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a limit cycle existed with constant value c, continuity and spiraling would force H to be constant on an open set — contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: strict Liapunov function forbids limit cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is a strict Liapunov function for a planar system, then there are no limit cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Liapunov function theory (decreasing along trajectories) developed earlier; used to rule out oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: homoclinic ω-limit set (possibility beyond closed orbits)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ω-limit set can consist of a saddle point together with one or two homoclinic solutions that leave and return to the saddle (example system provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that closed and bounded limit sets other than closed orbits or equilibria can be unions of equilibria and connecting orbits (homoclinic/heteroclinic).

rubrics_metrics.name: SIR model: reduced planar system and equilibria/stability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the basic SIR model with constant total population, reducing to (S,I) gives equilibria along I=0. Linearization at (S,0) yields eigenvalues 0 and βS−ν, so the sign of βS−ν determines the nonzero eigenvalue's stability (negative for S<ν/β, positive for S>ν/β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: threshold S=ν/β separates initial conditions where infection decays versus initially grows. Nullclines and phase portrait (I+S−(ν/β)log S constant along trajectories) provide more qualitative info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant (first-integral) for SIR trajectories
rubrics_metrics.description: Along solutions of the SIR reduced system, the quantity I + S − (ν/β) log S is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by separating variables dI/dS = −1 + ν/(βS) and integrating; yields uniqueness of solution curves connecting equilibria across the vertical nullcline S=ν/β and phase-portrait structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIRS model: existence and formula for nontrivial equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: In the SIRS model with total population τ, equilibria include (τ,0) and (S^*, I^*) with S^*=ν/β and I^*=μ(τ − ν/β)/(ν+μ) (expressions given in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equilibrium expressions identify parameter-dependent steady states; further linearization and nullcline analysis determine their stability and bifurcations (exercises prompt this).
